title: Fluctuating student motivation and what we can do about it o-about-it/
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino starts from her own experience: since becoming a teacher she cannot read when mentally exhausted, and she reads obsessively when rested. She uses this to explain why students who want to try are still not equally motivated every lesson. Because a student who drifts through one lesson then feels lost in the next, small lapses compound into lasting demotivation. Since a teacher cannot guarantee full motivation in every student, she aims to keep participation high so that success remains within reach. Her practical routine covers attention cues, predictable openers, quiet check-ins, breaking up tasks, whole-class response on mini-whiteboards and processing time. She ends with the role of honesty in classroom culture, admitting to students that focus is a struggle for her too.
points: Fluctuating motivation compounds: a lesson missed mentally leaves the student lost next time, which makes demotivation more likely.
Securing attention first, with cues at transitions and by removing distractions such as corridor noise, comes before anything else.
Delaying instructions, such as not revealing the pair discussion until students have written on mini-whiteboards, ensures every step is completed properly.
Chunking independent practice into shorter sets for tired or end-of-week classes gives easier targets and renews focus.
Admitting to students that focusing is hard for the teacher too lends weight to strategies like rehearsal.
quotes: Success is clearly an important lever in motivating students. When students feel success is attainable, they are more likely to be motivated to learn.

The next time they get to the lesson, they are feeling a little more motivated but because they didn’t register what was going on in the previous lesson, they feel lost and struggle to keep up as quickly as the others in the room. Over time, this builds up and this student is likely to feel demotivated more often.

Familiarity of routines means the actual learning is main focus in the classroom. When a student walks in, feeling tired or demotivated, a task they are used to means they feel less uncertainty. But a routine, particularly one at the beginning of a lesson, also provides students time to recentre themselves, time to attune themselves to the new lesson and environment they find themselves in.

If I know I want students to Turn and Talk about something, I don’t reveal this straightaway. First, I ask students to think and write down their thoughts on their mini-whiteboard. Once they have done this, I then reveal that they will be discussing their answers in pairs. By delaying some instructions, I can ensure all students are completing each step properly. This, together with front-loading the means of participation, helps students participate fully.

The best way to ensure all students are participating is to use whole class response to gauge student focus, retention and understanding. I use mini-whiteboards throughout a lesson and have a strict routine to check responses so that all students are thinking about and answering questions. I encourage students to put a question mark if they don’t know an answer so I know what I need to re-explain.

Sometimes, lessons can be fast-paced and students are expected to move from one task to another seamlessly. This can be difficult when they may be demotivated because they are tired or have been thinking hard all day or have missed a few lessons or feel that success is elusive. Allowing students a bit of time to think about, process what they have just learnt and rehearse it themselves means we slow things down enough for them to feel the learning is within their grasp.

But one aspect that I think is very important in developing the right culture is honesty. When I sense my students losing focus, I acknowledge that focusing all the time can be a struggle for me too and that I try to refocus and give myself time to think about something fully. This then also lends weight to the strategies I use in the classroom, such as rehearsal, as my students can see the thinking behind them.
